title: COLUMN: The Mysterious Phenomenon Surrounding Near-Death Experiences
excerpt: What happens after death? People who have come back to life share stories of mysterious experiences that raise questions about the afterlife
content:

What actually happens when we die—and can our consciousness live on after our heart stops beating? This column explores the mysterious phenomenon of near-death experiences, the research behind them, and people’s astonishing accounts of what awaits on the other side.

In life, there are certain questions that are universal to all of us humans, and sooner or later we ask ourselves the big questions, such as “What happens when we die?” For death is one of the things that is certain—an absolute. So what happens when we die? Some say that our consciousness ceases as soon as our organs stop functioning, while others say that our consciousness—or soul—does not die but continues to live on. That it is only the body that dies. There are also those who say that we can never really know until we die ourselves, and that it’s impossible to know what will happen. And then there’s a mysterious phenomenon known as near-death experiences.

Since death is such a natural and common process, there are also those who die and come back, and they bring with them a whole story about what they experienced while they were on the other side.

These stories recur time and again throughout human history, across all ages, genders, cultures, religions, and ethnicities, and even among people with various disabilities, such as blindness.

Today, there are doctors and other specialists who have chosen to explore this rare phenomenon. They study individuals who claim to have had what is known as a near-death experience. Although the experience itself is unique to each individual, researchers have been able to identify similarities and patterns among them. One of the individuals who has chosen to study this is Dr. Jeffrey Long.

Dr. Jeffrey Long’s case study of more than 5,000 individuals

Dr. Jeffrey Long is a practicing physician and the author of the New York Times bestseller *Evidence of the Afterlife*. Throughout his career, he encountered individuals who reported having near-death experiences, which inspired him to begin studying the phenomenon. Among other things, he launched a website to collect these case studies. This website features a questionnaire with a large number of in-depth questions. The website was launched more than 25 years ago and has now collected over 5,000 case studies of near-death experiences. https://www.nderf.org/index.htm

What is the definition of a near-death experience?

Dr. Jeffrey Long explained in an interview with Theo Von on his podcast *This Past Weekend* that the definition of a near-death experience is exactly what it sounds like—being close to death. It’s when the body is so physically compromised that you’re either unconscious or clinically dead, with no heartbeat. At that point, it should be impossible to have any kind of clear, conscious memories, yet these people still have these recollections. When the body goes into cardiac arrest and the heart stops pumping blood, blood flow to the brain ceases within 10–20 seconds. An EEG (electroencephalogram), which measures the brain’s electrical activity, is completely interrupted at that point. At that point, there is no longer any measurable cortical brain activity. There have also been cases where people have had these near-death experiences while under general anesthesia. Anyone who has been under general anesthesia knows that the brain should be completely shut down.

Overwhelming agreement

Based on his studies, Dr. Jeffrey Long noticed, even in the first dozen accounts, an overwhelming consistency in characteristics and traits that typically occur in a coherent and logical order. It bore no resemblance to anything that might be associated with dreams or drug-induced hallucinations.

These are some of the common scenarios:

  1. Life-threatening incident When the body is so physically compromised that the person is either unconscious or clinically dead with no heartbeat
  2. Out-of-body experience It is when consciousness separates from the body and observes its surroundings
  3. You can walk through a tunnel, and at the end of the tunnel there is a beautiful light that leads to what is described as a heavenly or otherworldly place
  4. Encounters with Deceased Loved Ones
  5. Life Review That's when you relive your life, either in part or in its entirety. It's common to experience it from your own perspective as well as from others' perspectives at the same time.
  6. The decision of whether to remain in this heavenly, otherworldly place or to return to one's life on Earth When the body is usually in a critical condition.

Other common characteristics from the near-death experience study:

  • That this heavenly or otherworldly place is usually described as non-physical, and that movement is also non-physical
  • Communication is almost always telepathic
  • Time is described as either nonexistent or radically different from that on Earth
  • The scenery and colors are so incredibly beautiful that it's hard to describe in words
  • When consciousness separates from the body, it is common to feel a sense of calm and peace
  • A feeling that this is their “true” self or real self when their consciousness is separated from their body
  • Around 93.81 TP3T reported that the experience they had on the other side felt much more real than their lives on Earth
  • a sense of unconditional and boundless love

Evidence

In addition to the study Dr. Long conducted with over 5,000 case studies—which is the largest study ever conducted on near-death experiences—there are other ways to prove that this is a real phenomenon. After all, one could always argue that anyone could answer a questionnaire, even if the responses are honest.

He explains that the evidence lies in the out-of-body state, also known as an out-of-body experience (OBE). When consciousness separates from the body, it is common to begin observing one’s surroundings. Dr. Long and other researchers have investigated how accurate these observations are during out-of-body states, and amazingly, over 98% of the observations in his study match down to the smallest detail. The fact is that they can make these observations from a location geographically far removed from their body or any form of possible sensory awareness. Although it sounds unbelievable, these scientific and consistent results have been confirmed. This means, therefore, that an individual’s body can be in one place while the observation is made several kilometers away.

One example of such an observation is Pam Reynolds’ near-death experience from 1991, which is one of the best-known, most well-documented, and most scientifically debated cases. Reynolds underwent an extremely risky brain surgery to repair an aneurysm in her brainstem. The surgery involved lowering the patient’s body temperature to 15 degrees. This was done to stop the heart and breathing and to drain all the blood from the brain. Reynolds was clinically dead for about an hour but then recovered to a stable condition once the surgery was complete.

Even though she showed no signs of heart or brain activity at various points during the surgery and while under anesthesia, Pam Reynolds had a clear and detailed recollection of her own surgery, what the doctors and other medical staff were doing, their conversations with one another, and what was on the operating table. She also remembers being led up toward the light through a kind of tunnel and meeting deceased loved ones. She then chose to return to earthly life and her body. (For a more detailed article about Pam Reynolds’ experience, visit https://psi-encyclopedia.spr.ac.uk/articles/pam-reynolds-near-death-experience/)

Lena's near-death experience

To gain a deeper understanding of this phenomenon, I asked the only person I personally know who has had a near-death experience. Her name is Lena, and this is her story in her own words.

On November 11, 1991, I had an NDE. My children were just over 4 months and just over 1.5 years old when I developed sepsis at the age of 30. The sepsis progressed to the point where I actually died in the intensive care unit at Sweden’s largest university hospital. The doctors have explained that two miracles occurred. One was that I survived, because there are no reported cases anywhere in the world of anyone surviving such advanced sepsis.

The second thing is that I didn’t suffer any injuries whatsoever as a result of the blood poisoning, which was confirmed by several more or less advanced tests, such as those using radioactive isotopes. After this experience, my life changed in many ways, but it has been—and still is—a struggle to become the best version of myself that I feel I can be.

This is my experience:

After I was admitted to the intensive care unit with severe pain throughout my body and hooked up to monitoring equipment, my condition quickly deteriorated. The last reading I heard of my body temperature was 41.3 degrees Celsius, which caused the staff to gather around me. I was on an IV drip with two different antibiotics, and the doctors told me that it didn’t seem to be helping; then three different surgeons came in, one after another, wanting to operate to remove one organ after another. I refused and shouted at them, ”If you stick a knife in me, I’ll die!”. As someone with advanced medical training, I knew that the cascade of reactions the body triggers after surgery on an infected body would definitely spell the end for me, and finally, the last of them replied, ””We’ll wash our hands, and it’s at your own risk,’ and all that remained were the nurses and the intensive care doctor.”.

My heart was racing (tachycardia), and it felt like an elephant was sitting on my chest. I wanted to drink water because it felt like the pain would ease if I could burp. I wasn’t allowed to drink, I was told, in case I needed emergency surgery. But two of the nurses stood on either side of me, raised the head of the bed slightly, took hold of me under each arm, and asked me to push off with my feet so I could move further up in the bed. Then something strange happened: as I pushed off with my feet, a neon-green image ”floated” up—first my feet, and then the rest of my body slowly followed.

As the green energy worked its way upward and ”settled” like a reflection of my body about 15–20 cm above my ”physical body,” the pain subsided, and it was such an enormous relief when it reached my chest and the ”elephant” disappeared. When it was time for my head to be ”separated,” there was a popping sound, and everything went black. Below me, I heard the nurses talking and saying, ”What a shame! She had such young children.” My immediate thought was, ”Had… How lucky that I’ve taken out life insurance.” Then I began to figure out where I was. It was an upward-sloping tunnel, like the inside of an intestine but made of black velvet, and I could see how it moved slowly and how the ”folds” shifted slightly. I was lying on my back and could see my toes and feel my long hair swaying beneath me from a gentle current of air that reminded me of a summer breeze. I was wearing a white nightgown, and I felt happier and more loved than I had ever felt in my life up to that point.

I thought about my children, and as I brought them to mind, I was able to ”step into” their lives and flip back and forth through them as if they were a deck of cards. I could pause, enter a ”scene” or moment, and feel what they were experiencing and thinking. I followed them all the way into their teenage years and noted that, while they would indeed be somewhat limited in their development and maturity, they would still manage just fine without me. I felt my eyes fill with tears as they streamed down my temples, and I knew I could let go and return HOME. I felt an inner sense of jubilation and joy and set off upward through the ”velvet tunnel,” which seemed to lead out into space, for I could make out stars and light at the opening. Then everything went black.

I woke up in a hospital bed in the ICU, where I had to stay for a couple of days, and I was so sad that I had returned to my body. My hospital stay lasted a total of one month, and during the first few weeks, I cried several times a day. I was so weak, and a third of my red blood cells had been destroyed by the sepsis, so I was yellow rather than pale. It took me several years before I could talk about my experience, because the spiritual transformation was brutal and difficult to accept for an academic trained in the natural sciences. Now, 35 years after my NDE, I can confidently say that there is a life before and a completely different life after that event, and I have fully accepted who I am and have used the knowledge I gained about my children’s lives without me to guide them in becoming the best versions of themselves.

Summary and Personal Thoughts

There are also organizations and platforms dedicated to sharing and studying this unique and extraordinary phenomenon. Organizations such as the International Association for Near-Death Studies (iands), a North Carolina-based organization in the U.S. that helps people who have had near-death experiences. There are even entire YouTube channels dedicated solely to letting people share their near-death experiences. Channels such as IANDS, Coming Home, The Other Side NDE, Shaman Oaks, and many more.

Personally, I wonder why this research hasn't received more attention, even though the evidence is so significant—given the large-scale nature of the case study—and because it is a widely experienced and common phenomenon.

Perhaps it’s because we live in a very materialistic paradigm, and anything beyond the five senses of perception is dismissed as fantasy. However, many of these NDU videos have millions of views, so it seems there is a natural curiosity among many people.

Although near-death experiences are a fascinating phenomenon and truly deserve more recognition—including from the academic and scientific communities—it is even more interesting how a near-death experience drastically and intensely changes the individual who undergoes it. They are not the same person they were when they return. It can even be painful to return, and it can take a long time to process the experience and continue one’s life here on Earth.
